sectionTitle: The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: The Haber process is used to manufacture ammonia, which can be used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.
The raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.
Students should be able to recall a source for the nitrogen and a source for the hydrogen used in the Haber process.

The purified gases are passed over a catalyst of iron at a high temperature (about 450°C) and a high pressure (about 200 atmospheres). Some of the hydrogen and nitrogen reacts to form ammonia. The reaction is reversible so some of the ammonia produced breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen:
On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed. The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled.
(HT only) Students should be able to:
interpret graphs of reaction conditions versus rate
apply the principles of dynamic equilibrium in Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium to the Haber process
explain the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium
explain how the commercially used conditions for the Haber process are related to the availability and cost of raw materials and energy supplies, control of equilibrium position and rate.
Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are used as fertilisers to improve agricultural productivity. NPK fertilisers contain compounds of all three elements.

Industrial production of NPK fertilisers can be achieved using a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes. NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.
Ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are obtained by mining, but phosphate rock cannot be used directly as a fertiliser.
Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid or sulfuric acid to produce soluble salts that can be used as fertilisers.
recall the names of the salts produced when phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid, sulfuric acid and phosphoric acid
compare the industrial production of fertilisers with laboratory preparations of the same compounds, given appropriate information.

concepts.definition: The industrial process used to manufacture ammonia. Nitrogen and hydrogen are passed over an iron catalyst at about 450°C and about 200 atmospheres. The ammonia made can be used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.

A nitrogen-containing compound added to soil so that crops grow better. Ammonia from the Haber process is the starting material: it is used to make ammonium salts and nitric acid, which supply nitrogen to plants.

concepts.term: Raw materials of the Haber process
concepts.definition: The two raw materials are nitrogen and hydrogen. No other reactant is fed into the reaction vessel.
The nitrogen is obtained from the air, which is about 80% nitrogen.
The hydrogen is obtained from natural gas, which is mainly methane. (Hydrogen obtained from other hydrocarbons is also an acceptable source.)
The nitrogen and hydrogen are purified before they enter the reaction vessel. Impurities would coat the iron catalyst and stop it working, so the gases passed over the catalyst are purified gases.

A catalyst of iron is used. It speeds up the rate at which the reaction reaches equilibrium. It does not change the position of equilibrium, so it does not change the percentage of ammonia in the mixture at equilibrium, and it is not used up.
The purified gases are passed over the iron catalyst at a high temperature (about 450°C) and a high pressure (about 200 atmospheres).

Some of the hydrogen and nitrogen reacts to form ammonia, and some of the ammonia produced breaks down again into nitrogen and hydrogen. Because the reaction is reversible, the gases leaving the reactor are always a mixture of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia.

concepts.term: Word equation for the Haber process
concepts.definition: The specification gives the reaction as: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonia. The ⇌ sign shows that the reaction is reversible.

The same reaction written in symbols is N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. Three molecules of hydrogen react with one molecule of nitrogen to give two molecules of ammonia, so there are 4 molecules of gas on the left and 2 on the right.

The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than nitrogen and hydrogen, so on cooling the ammonia liquefies and is removed while the other two gases stay as gases.

The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled: they are passed back into the reactor rather than thrown away. This means the raw materials are used efficiently even though only some of the gas reacts on each pass.

concepts.term: Interpreting graphs of conditions against rate
concepts.definition: On a graph of rate against temperature the rate rises as the temperature rises, because particles collide more often and with more energy. On a graph of rate against pressure the rate rises as the pressure rises, because the particles are closer together and collide more often. Read the axes first: a rate graph does not tell you the yield.

Equilibrium is reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions are taking place at exactly the same rate. Both reactions are still happening, but the amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia stay constant. The amounts are not equal to each other.

concepts.term: Effect of pressure on the position of equilibrium
concepts.definition: There are 4 molecules of gas on the left of N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 and 2 on the right. Increasing the pressure moves the position of equilibrium towards the side with fewer molecules of gas, so a higher pressure gives a higher percentage yield of ammonia.

concepts.term: Effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium
concepts.definition: The forward reaction that forms ammonia is exothermic. Raising the temperature moves the position of equilibrium in the endothermic direction, that is, back towards nitrogen and hydrogen, so a higher temperature gives a lower percentage yield of ammonia.

Ammonia is removed from the mixture as it liquefies. Removing a product moves the position of equilibrium to the right, so more nitrogen and hydrogen react and the process keeps producing ammonia rather than settling at a fixed composition.

concepts.term: Trade-off between rate and position of equilibrium
concepts.definition: A low temperature would give a high yield of ammonia but the reaction would be far too slow to be useful; a high temperature is fast but the yield is low. About 450°C is a compromise: it gives a lower yield than a cold reactor would, but it produces ammonia quickly enough, and the unreacted gases are recycled.

A higher pressure increases both the rate and the yield, so the pressure used is limited only by cost and safety. Very high pressures need thick, strong pipes and vessels and a great deal of energy to compress the gas, so about 200 atmospheres is used as a compromise.

concepts.term: Availability and cost of raw materials
concepts.definition: Nitrogen is taken from the air, which is freely available; hydrogen has to be made from natural gas, which must be bought. Recycling the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen keeps the cost of raw materials down, but fresh raw materials are still needed as ammonia is removed.

Energy is needed to heat the gases to about 450°C and to compress them to about 200 atmospheres, and energy costs money. The commercial conditions are chosen to make ammonia at an acceptable rate and yield for an acceptable overall cost, not to give the highest possible yield.
A fertiliser containing compounds of all three of the elements nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Compounds of these elements are used as fertilisers to improve agricultural productivity.

NPK fertilisers are formulations: mixtures of various salts, blended in measured quantities so that the fertiliser contains appropriate percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium for the crop and soil.

Industrial production of NPK fertilisers uses a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes. Different salts are made in linked stages on the same site, and the products are then blended.

Ammonia is a base and is neutralised by acids to make ammonium salts, for example ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate, and ammonia + sulfuric acid → ammonium sulfate. These salts supply nitrogen to plants.
Ammonia is also used as the raw material for manufacturing nitric acid. The nitric acid made can then be reacted with more ammonia to make ammonium nitrate, or used to treat phosphate rock.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are all obtained by mining. Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are soluble salts, so they can be used as fertilisers as they are.

concepts.term: Why phosphate rock cannot be used directly
concepts.definition: Phosphate rock cannot be used directly as a fertiliser because it is insoluble in water, so plants cannot take the phosphorus in through their roots. It must first be turned into soluble salts.

Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid or sulfuric acid to produce soluble salts that can be used as fertilisers. The acid does not add phosphorus; it converts the phosphorus already in the rock into a soluble form.
Treating phosphate rock with nitric acid produces phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate. Both are soluble, and the phosphoric acid can be neutralised with ammonia to make ammonium phosphate.
Treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid produces single superphosphate, which is a mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate.
Treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid produces triple superphosphate, which is calcium phosphate.

concepts.term: Industrial production compared with laboratory preparation
concepts.definition: In the laboratory an ammonium salt is made in a batch by titrating dilute ammonia solution with a dilute acid and then crystallising the pure salt. In industry the same salt is made continuously, on a very large scale, from hot concentrated solutions, in stages integrated with the processes that make the ammonia and the acid.

misconceptions.question: What does the Haber process actually make?
misconceptions.correct: The Haber process manufactures ammonia. The ammonia is then used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers in further reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: The Haber process makes fertiliser - the ammonia is the fertiliser that gets spread on fields.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Haber process is always introduced in the context of feeding the world, so students join the two ideas together and skip the step in between. Ammonia is also sometimes described loosely as 'fertiliser feedstock'.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia is the product of the Haber process. It must be reacted further - for example with nitric acid to make ammonium nitrate - before it becomes a fertiliser.

misconceptions.question: Which two gases are fed into the Haber process?
misconceptions.correct: Nitrogen and hydrogen. These are the raw materials named in the specification.
misconceptions.misconception: Nitrogen and oxygen, because both of them come out of the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that one raw material comes from the air, and the air gas they meet most often alongside nitrogen is oxygen. Fractional distillation of liquid air is also taught as a source of both gases.
misconceptions.correction: Only the nitrogen comes from the air. The second raw material is hydrogen, which is obtained from natural gas. Oxygen is not used at all.

misconceptions.question: Where do the two raw materials come from?
misconceptions.correct: Nitrogen is obtained from the air; hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane).
misconceptions.misconception: Both gases are taken out of the air, or the two sources belong the other way round - nitrogen from natural gas and hydrogen from the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pair of sources is memorised as a list without meaning, so it is easy to swap. Students also know that air is a mixture of gases and assume hydrogen is one of them.
misconceptions.correction: There is almost no hydrogen in the air. Hydrogen must be manufactured from a hydrocarbon, normally methane in natural gas. Nitrogen is the gas that comes from the air.

misconceptions.question: Where is the nitrogen for the Haber process obtained?
misconceptions.correct: From the air, which is about 80% nitrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Nitrogen is dug out of the ground as nitrate rock and then broken down, in the way that phosphate rock is mined for phosphorus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The fertiliser topic covers mining of phosphate rock and potassium salts, so students generalise and assume every element in a fertiliser starts in a mine.
misconceptions.correction: Nitrogen is different from phosphorus and potassium here: it is taken from the air, which is a free and unlimited supply. Only the potassium salts and phosphate rock are mined.

misconceptions.question: Does the iron catalyst increase the amount of ammonia made at equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: No. The catalyst increases the rate of the reaction, so equilibrium is reached faster, but it does not change the position of equilibrium or the percentage yield.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst makes more ammonia, because a catalyst makes the reaction work better.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Speeds up' and 'makes more' are treated as the same thing in everyday language, and students see that a factory with a catalyst produces more ammonia per day - which is a rate effect, not a yield effect.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the composition at equilibrium is unchanged. It changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not what the equilibrium is.

misconceptions.question: Which catalyst is used in the Haber process?
misconceptions.correct: A catalyst of iron.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst is nickel, or platinum.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nickel is the catalyst used for hydrogenating vegetable oils and platinum appears in catalytic converters, so students recall a catalyst without recalling which reaction it belongs to.
misconceptions.correction: The Haber process uses an iron catalyst. Nickel belongs to the hydrogenation of unsaturated oils, not to ammonia manufacture.

misconceptions.question: What temperature and pressure are used in the Haber process?
misconceptions.correct: A high temperature of about 450°C and a high pressure of about 200 atmospheres.
misconceptions.misconception: About 200°C and about 450 atmospheres.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two numbers, 450 and 200, are learned as bare figures with no reason attached, so they are easily attached to the wrong quantity.
misconceptions.correction: The figures are about 450°C and about 200 atmospheres. Tie each number to a reason: 450°C is a compromise temperature, and 200 atmospheres is as high a pressure as it is safe and affordable to use.

misconceptions.question: Does all the nitrogen and hydrogen turn into ammonia?
misconceptions.correct: No. The reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down again into nitrogen and hydrogen, and the gas leaving the reactor is a mixture of all three.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction runs until the nitrogen and hydrogen are used up, because that is what reactions do - the ⇌ sign just means it could be reversed later if you wanted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every equation met before this topic uses a single arrow and goes to completion, so the reversible arrow is read as an ordinary arrow with a note attached rather than as two reactions happening at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: ⇌ means the forward and reverse reactions are both happening at the same time in the same vessel. The reactants can never be fully used up, which is exactly why unreacted gases have to be recycled.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?
misconceptions.correct: They are recycled: the remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are passed back into the reactor.
misconceptions.misconception: They are waste gases, so they are burned off or released into the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture a factory chimney and assume anything that is not the product is waste. The word 'unreacted' sounds like 'left over'.
misconceptions.correction: Nitrogen and hydrogen cost money and energy to obtain, so they are fed back round the loop. Recycling is the reason a low yield per pass is still commercially acceptable.

misconceptions.question: How is the ammonia separated from the mixture?
misconceptions.correct: The mixture is cooled. The ammonia liquefies and is removed, while the nitrogen and hydrogen remain as gases.
misconceptions.misconception: Cooling turns the ammonia into a solid that can be shovelled out, or cooling turns the whole mixture into liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know cooling a gas condenses it but do not compare boiling points, so they either take the change too far to a solid, or apply it to all three gases at once.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia has a far higher boiling point than nitrogen and hydrogen, so it is the only one that condenses at the temperature used. It is removed as a liquid, not as a solid.

misconceptions.question: Does recycling mean no fresh raw materials are needed?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ammonia is continually removed from the loop, so fresh nitrogen and hydrogen must be fed in continuously to replace the atoms that leave as ammonia.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the leftover gases go round again, the plant only needs one batch of nitrogen and hydrogen to keep running.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Recycled' is heard as 'reused for ever'. Students do not track where the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms in the removed ammonia have come from.
misconceptions.correction: Every tonne of ammonia taken out of the loop removes nitrogen and hydrogen atoms from it. Recycling reduces waste; it does not remove the need to buy raw materials.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of ammonia?
misconceptions.correct: Ammonia is NH3. The equation is N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonia is NH4, and ammonia and ammonium mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ammonium ion NH4+ appears throughout the fertiliser topic, in ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate, and the two words differ by only two letters.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia is the neutral molecule NH3. Ammonium, NH4+, is the ion formed when ammonia gains a hydrogen ion from an acid, and it is only found in compounds such as ammonium nitrate.

misconceptions.question: At equilibrium, have the reactions stopped?
misconceptions.correct: No. At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, but at exactly the same rate, so the amounts of each substance stay constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium means the reaction has finished and everything has stopped moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The observable evidence - concentrations that no longer change - looks exactly like a reaction that has ended, and 'equilibrium' suggests stillness in everyday use.
misconceptions.correction: This is why it is called a dynamic equilibrium. Nitrogen and hydrogen keep making ammonia and ammonia keeps breaking down; the two rates simply cancel out.

misconceptions.question: At equilibrium, are the amounts of reactants and products equal?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the rates of the forward and reverse reactions that are equal. The amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia are constant but usually very different from each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium means there is the same amount of each substance, like a balanced see-saw.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'equilibrium' and the balance imagery used to introduce it both suggest equal quantities on the two sides.
misconceptions.correction: Equal rates, not equal amounts. In the Haber process only a modest percentage of the mixture at equilibrium is ammonia, which is why the ammonia is removed and the rest recycled.

misconceptions.question: Does pressure affect the yield of ammonia, or only the rate?
misconceptions.correct: Increasing the pressure increases the rate and also moves the position of equilibrium towards ammonia, so it increases the yield.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure just squashes the particles together so they collide more often; it cannot change how much ammonia you end up with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is first met in the rates topic, where its only role is collision frequency, so students carry that single explanation into the equilibrium topic.
misconceptions.correction: Where the numbers of gas molecules differ on the two sides of the equation, pressure also changes the position of equilibrium. Here there are 4 molecules of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so higher pressure gives more ammonia.

misconceptions.question: Which way does increasing the pressure move the equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the side with fewer molecules of gas, which is the ammonia side, so the yield of ammonia increases.
misconceptions.misconception: Squeezing the gases pushes the equilibrium towards nitrogen and hydrogen, because that side has more molecules crowded into the space.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that the crowded side must be favoured by squeezing, rather than that the system relieves the pressure by reducing the number of molecules.
misconceptions.correction: The system responds by moving to the side that occupies less volume - the side with fewer gas molecules. Count the molecules: 1 + 3 on the left, 2 on the right, so higher pressure favours ammonia.

misconceptions.question: What is the effect of removing ammonia as it is formed?
misconceptions.correct: Removing the ammonia moves the position of equilibrium to the right, so more nitrogen and hydrogen react to replace it.
misconceptions.misconception: Taking the ammonia away leaves less product, so the reaction makes less ammonia overall, or it stops because the equilibrium is broken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think about the snapshot - less ammonia in the vessel - rather than about how the system responds to the change over time.
misconceptions.correction: Removing a product means the reverse reaction has less to work with, so the forward reaction dominates until equilibrium is restored. Continuous removal keeps the process converting the raw materials.

misconceptions.question: If the rate rises as the temperature rises, does the yield rise too?
misconceptions.correct: No. Raising the temperature raises the rate but lowers the percentage yield of ammonia, because the forward reaction is exothermic.
misconceptions.misconception: The rate graph and the yield graph must go the same way - if one line rises with temperature, so does the other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both graphs have temperature on the x-axis and look similar at a glance, and students expect 'better conditions' to improve everything at once.
misconceptions.correction: Always read the y-axis. Rate against temperature rises; percentage yield against temperature falls. The fact that they pull in opposite directions is the whole reason a compromise temperature is needed.

misconceptions.question: Why is the yield of ammonia lower at a higher temperature?
misconceptions.correct: The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature moves the position of equilibrium in the endothermic direction, back towards nitrogen and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: A higher temperature must give more ammonia, because heating always makes a reaction produce more product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In every rates experiment students have done, heating gives more product in the time allowed. That is a rate effect, and it is being applied to a question about equilibrium position.
misconceptions.correction: Heating gets you to equilibrium faster but shifts that equilibrium the wrong way. More ammonia per minute at first, but a smaller percentage of ammonia in the mixture once equilibrium is reached.

misconceptions.question: If high pressure improves both rate and yield, why not use a far higher pressure?
misconceptions.correct: Very high pressures need thick, strong pipes and vessels and a great deal of energy to compress the gas, so they are expensive and less safe. About 200 atmospheres is a compromise.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure should simply be as high as possible, because there is no chemical reason not to.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly work out that pressure helps both rate and yield, then stop, because the limiting reasons are economic and practical rather than chemical.
misconceptions.correction: The chemistry does favour higher pressure; the plant does not. Building and maintaining equipment that withstands very high pressure, and running the compressors, cost more than the extra ammonia is worth.

misconceptions.question: Are the raw materials for the Haber process free?
misconceptions.correct: No. Nitrogen from the air is freely available, but hydrogen has to be manufactured from natural gas, which must be bought, and energy supplies also cost money.
misconceptions.misconception: Both raw materials cost nothing, so the only expense is building the plant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Nitrogen comes from the air' is remembered as the headline fact, and hydrogen is quietly assumed to come from somewhere equally free.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen from natural gas is a real and significant cost, as is the energy used to heat and compress the gases. The conditions chosen have to balance these costs against the value of the ammonia produced.

misconceptions.question: Since the unreacted gases are recycled, does the yield matter?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A low yield per pass means more gas must be recycled, compressed and reheated each time, which costs energy and money, so conditions are chosen to balance yield against rate and cost.
misconceptions.misconception: Recycling means nothing is lost, so the yield is irrelevant and the plant should just run as fast as possible.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is presented as the solution to the low yield, so students conclude that the low yield has been cancelled out entirely.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling recovers the material but not the energy. Every recycled pass has to be compressed and heated again, so a very low yield makes ammonia more expensive even though no atoms are wasted.

misconceptions.question: What does an NPK fertiliser contain?
misconceptions.correct: Compounds of all three elements - nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium - not the elements themselves.
misconceptions.misconception: An NPK fertiliser contains nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as the pure elements, mixed together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The label 'NPK' names elements, so students picture the elements themselves rather than their compounds, and the difference between an element and its compounds is easily blurred.
misconceptions.correction: Plants take up soluble ions, not elements. Potassium metal reacts violently with water and phosphorus is not usable in its elemental form; the fertiliser contains salts such as potassium sulfate and ammonium phosphate.

misconceptions.question: Is an NPK fertiliser a single compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. NPK fertilisers are formulations - mixtures of various salts, blended so that the fertiliser contains appropriate percentages of the three elements.
misconceptions.misconception: NPK is one compound with nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium all in the same formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single label 'NPK fertiliser' and the single bag it is sold in suggest a single substance, and students have met few formulations by this point.
misconceptions.correction: It is a formulation. Different salts supply the different elements, and the proportions are varied to suit the crop and the soil, which no single compound could do.

misconceptions.question: Is an NPK fertiliser made in one reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Industrial production uses a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes; the separate salts are made in linked stages and then blended.
misconceptions.misconception: There is one big reaction in one vessel that turns the raw materials straight into NPK fertiliser.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are used to a single equation representing a single industrial process, so a product made from several separate salts does not fit the pattern.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia is made by the Haber process, nitric acid from ammonia, ammonium salts from ammonia and acids, and phosphate rock is treated with acid - all on the same site, feeding into one another.

misconceptions.question: What is formed when ammonia reacts with nitric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Ammonium nitrate only. Ammonia is a base that accepts a hydrogen ion: NH3 + HNO3 → NH4NO3.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonia and nitric acid give ammonium nitrate and water, because acid + base always gives a salt and water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'acid + base → salt + water' is learned for metal oxides and hydroxides, where the water comes from the hydroxide, and is then applied to ammonia without checking where the oxygen and hydrogen would come from.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia contains no oxygen and no hydroxide ion, so no water can be formed. The ammonia simply gains a hydrogen ion from the acid to become the ammonium ion, and one salt is the only product.

misconceptions.question: What is the salt made when ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Ammonium sulfate.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonium sulfide, or ammonium sulfite, because the acid is sulfuric acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The names sound alike and students match the salt to the acid by ear rather than by working out the ion. Sulfide and sulfite are met in other contexts and are easy to reach for.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, contains the sulfate ion SO4 2-, so its salts are sulfates. Sulfides come from hydrogen sulfide and sulfites from sulfurous acid.

misconceptions.question: Can phosphate rock be spread onto fields as it is?
misconceptions.correct: No. Phosphate rock cannot be used directly as a fertiliser; it must be treated with an acid to make soluble salts.
misconceptions.misconception: Phosphate rock contains phosphorus, so it can be crushed and spread straight onto the fields.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is mined like the potassium salts, which can be used directly, so students treat all three mined materials the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Phosphate rock is insoluble in water, so plants cannot take the phosphorus in through their roots. Treating it with nitric or sulfuric acid produces the soluble salts that plants can absorb.

misconceptions.question: Do the mined potassium salts also have to be treated with acid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are soluble salts, so they can be used as fertilisers without further treatment.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything that comes out of a mine has to be reacted with acid before it can be used as a fertiliser.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The acid treatment of phosphate rock is the memorable step in this section, so it is generalised to the other mined materials.
misconceptions.correction: Only phosphate rock needs treating, because only phosphate rock is insoluble. The potassium salts dissolve in water and go straight into the formulation.

misconceptions.question: What does the acid do to the phosphate rock?
misconceptions.correct: It converts the insoluble phosphate already in the rock into soluble salts that plants can take up.
misconceptions.misconception: The acid adds the phosphorus to the rock, so without acid there would be no phosphorus in the fertiliser.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'phosphoric' appears in the acid used for triple superphosphate, so students conclude that the phosphorus is being supplied by the acid rather than released from the rock.
misconceptions.correction: The phosphorus is in the rock all along, locked up in an insoluble compound. The acid changes its solubility, and with nitric or sulfuric acid it supplies no phosphorus at all.

misconceptions.question: What is produced when phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.
misconceptions.misconception: Phosphoric acid, whichever acid is used - acid on phosphate rock always gives phosphoric acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only one of the three acid treatments produces phosphoric acid, but it is the most memorable product name in the section, so it is applied to all of them.
misconceptions.correction: Nitric acid gives phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate. Sulfuric acid gives single superphosphate, a mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate; phosphoric acid itself gives triple superphosphate, calcium phosphate.

misconceptions.question: Which acid produces triple superphosphate?
misconceptions.correct: Phosphoric acid. Sulfuric acid produces single superphosphate.
misconceptions.misconception: Sulfuric acid gives triple superphosphate, because sulfuric acid is the strongest and most widely used industrial acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three acids and their three products are learned as an unstructured list, and 'triple' is assumed to go with the acid that sounds most powerful.
misconceptions.correction: Link each product to the acid by its name: phosphoric acid adds more phosphate, giving the richer product, triple superphosphate, which is calcium phosphate. Sulfuric acid leaves calcium sulfate behind in the mixture, so its product is single superphosphate.

misconceptions.question: How does industrial production differ from the laboratory preparation of the same salt?
misconceptions.correct: The laboratory method is a small batch process using dilute solutions, titration and crystallisation to give a pure salt; industry runs a continuous process on a huge scale using hot concentrated solutions, integrated with the processes that supply the reactants.
misconceptions.misconception: The industrial process is exactly the same method as the laboratory one, just carried out in much bigger containers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both make the same compound from the same reactants, so students assume the procedure must scale up unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Scale changes the method. Titrating and crystallising batch by batch would be far too slow and costly for thousands of tonnes, and the fertiliser does not need to be a pure crystalline salt, so industry uses concentrated solutions in a continuous process.

mcqs.stem: What is manufactured by the Haber process?

options.text: Ammonium nitrate fertiliser, ready to be spread onto fields
options.rationale: Students who join 'Haber process' straight to 'fertiliser' skip the step in which ammonia is reacted with an acid.

options.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen, which are separated out from the air
options.rationale: Confuses the raw materials with the product, and repeats the idea that both gases come from the air.

options.text: Nitric acid, which is sprayed onto crops to supply nitrogen
options.rationale: Nitric acid is made from ammonia later in the fertiliser industry, so its name is associated with the same topic.

options.text: Ammonia, which is then used to make nitrogen-based fertilisers
options.rationale: The Haber process manufactures ammonia; the ammonia is used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.

mcqs.stem: Which two raw materials are used in the Haber process, and where does each come from?

options.text: Nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas
options.rationale: These are the two raw materials and the sources students are required to be able to recall.

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen, both taken from the air
options.rationale: Oxygen is the air gas most often paired with nitrogen, so it displaces hydrogen.

options.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen, both taken from the air
options.rationale: The raw materials are right but the second source is wrong: there is almost no hydrogen in air.

options.text: Nitrogen from natural gas and hydrogen from air
options.rationale: The two sources are learned as a pair and swapped over.

mcqs.stem: Where is the nitrogen used in the Haber process obtained from?

options.text: From natural gas, by reacting methane with steam
options.rationale: This is the source of the hydrogen, attached to the wrong gas.

options.text: From nitrate rock, which is mined and then heated
options.rationale: Fits the pattern of the fertiliser topic, in which phosphate rock and potassium salts are mined.

options.text: From the air, which contains about 80% nitrogen
options.rationale: Air is the source of nitrogen, and it is freely available.

options.text: From ammonia, which is broken down again on the iron
options.rationale: Reads the reverse reaction as a way of supplying the reactants rather than as a limit on yield.

mcqs.stem: Where is the hydrogen used in the Haber process obtained from?

options.text: From the air, in the same way as the nitrogen
options.rationale: Assumes that both raw materials share one convenient source.

options.text: From the nitrogen, which is reacted with steam
options.rationale: Steam is associated with hydrogen manufacture, but nitrogen is not the substance it reacts with.

options.text: From the gases recycled back into the reactor
options.rationale: Treats the recycled gas as the source, forgetting that fresh raw materials must replace what leaves as ammonia.

options.text: From natural gas, which is mainly methane
options.rationale: Hydrogen is manufactured from a hydrocarbon; natural gas is the standard source.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?

options.text: About 450°C, about 200 atmospheres, nickel catalyst
options.rationale: The conditions are right but the catalyst is the one used for hydrogenating oils.

options.text: About 450°C, about 200 atmospheres, iron catalyst
options.rationale: These are the conditions given in the specification.

options.text: About 200°C, about 450 atmospheres, iron catalyst
options.rationale: The two numbers are recalled but attached to the wrong quantities.

options.text: About 25°C, about 200 atmospheres, iron catalyst
options.rationale: A student who knows a cooler reactor would give a higher yield assumes the coldest option is used.

mcqs.stem: Why is a catalyst of iron used in the Haber process?

options.text: It increases the amount of ammonia made at equilibrium
options.rationale: 'Speeds up' is read as 'makes more', so the catalyst is credited with a higher yield.

options.text: It speeds up the reaction without changing the yield
options.rationale: A catalyst increases the rate so equilibrium is reached faster; it does not alter the position of equilibrium.

options.text: It stops the ammonia breaking back down into the gases
options.rationale: Treats the catalyst as a way of switching off the reverse reaction.

options.text: It is used up, so more is added all the time
options.rationale: Catalysts are confused with reactants, which are consumed as the reaction proceeds.

mcqs.stem: Why does only some of the nitrogen and hydrogen turn into ammonia?

options.text: All of it reacts, because the catalyst makes it go to completion
options.rationale: Reads ⇌ as an ordinary arrow and assumes the reactants are used up.

options.text: The unreacted gases are removed and thrown away as waste
options.rationale: Explains the leftover gas by disposal rather than by the reverse reaction.

options.text: The reaction is reversible, so some ammonia breaks down again
options.rationale: Some of the ammonia produced breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen, so the reaction cannot go to completion.

options.text: The pressure of 200 atmospheres is too low for it all to react
options.rationale: Blames the numerical conditions rather than the reversibility of the reaction.

mcqs.stem: Which word equation represents the reaction in the Haber process?

options.text: nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
options.rationale: A single arrow says the reaction goes to completion, which it does not.

options.text: nitrogen + oxygen ⇌ ammonia
options.rationale: Substitutes the air gas students associate with nitrogen for the true raw material.

options.text: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonium
options.rationale: Confuses the neutral molecule ammonia with the ammonium ion found in its salts.

options.text: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonia
options.rationale: This is the equation as the specification gives it, with the reversible arrow.

mcqs.stem: Which is the balanced symbol equation for the Haber process?

options.rationale: Balanced, with 2 N and 6 H on each side, and reversible.

options.text: N2 + H2 ⇌ NH3
options.rationale: The formulae are right but the equation is not balanced, a very common slip when balancing is rushed.
Balanced but not reversible, so it does not show that ammonia breaks down again.
Uses NH4 as though it were ammonia; NH4 is not a substance, and the ammonium ion is NH4+.

mcqs.stem: How is the ammonia separated from the mixture leaving the reactor?

options.text: The mixture is cooled until the ammonia freezes into a solid
options.rationale: Takes the change of state one step too far, to a solid that could be shovelled out.

options.text: The mixture is cooled, so all three gases liquefy together
options.rationale: Applies condensation to the whole mixture without comparing boiling points.

options.text: The mixture is cooled, so the ammonia liquefies and is removed
options.rationale: Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than the other two gases, so cooling condenses it out.

options.text: The other gases are burned off, leaving the ammonia behind
options.rationale: Treats the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen as waste to be disposed of.

mcqs.stem: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?

options.text: They are recycled back into the reactor
options.rationale: The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled, so the raw materials are used efficiently.

options.text: They are released into the air as a waste gas
options.rationale: Anything that is not the product is pictured as going up the chimney.

options.text: They are liquefied along with the ammonia
options.rationale: Assumes cooling condenses every gas in the mixture.

options.text: They are burned to heat the reactor vessel
options.rationale: A plausible-sounding use for a 'waste' gas, but the gases are far too valuable to burn.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows how the rate of the Haber reaction changes as the temperature is raised at constant pressure. What does the graph show, and what does it not show?

options.text: The rate increases, and the yield of ammonia increases too
options.rationale: Applies rate reasoning to equilibrium position, so heating is assumed to improve everything.

options.text: The rate falls, in the same way as the yield of ammonia falls
options.rationale: Assumes the rate graph must follow the same shape as the yield graph.

options.text: The rate is unchanged once the iron catalyst has been added
options.rationale: Treats the catalyst as fixing the rate, so temperature is thought to make no difference.

options.text: The rate increases, although the yield of ammonia falls
options.rationale: Rate rises with temperature; the percentage yield falls because the forward reaction is exothermic.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows how the rate of the Haber reaction changes as the pressure is increased at constant temperature. Which description of the graph, with its reason, is correct?

options.text: The rate falls as pressure rises, because the gas particles are squashed
options.rationale: Reasons that squeezing hinders the particles rather than increasing their collision frequency.

options.text: The rate rises as pressure rises, because collisions are more frequent
options.rationale: Compressing the gases puts the molecules closer together, so they collide more often per second.

options.text: The rate is unchanged, because pressure only affects the yield
options.rationale: Splits the two effects the wrong way round: pressure affects rate as well as position of equilibrium.

options.text: The rate rises only once the temperature is above about 450°C
options.rationale: Attaches the effect to the memorised temperature figure instead of to the pressure axis.

mcqs.stem: Increasing the pressure increases the percentage yield of ammonia at equilibrium. Why?

options.text: There are fewer gas molecules on the ammonia side of the equation
options.rationale: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 has 4 molecules of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so higher pressure favours ammonia.

options.text: There are more gas molecules on the ammonia side of the equation
options.rationale: Counts the molecules the wrong way round, or assumes squeezing favours the crowded side.

options.text: Higher pressure speeds up only the forward reaction, not the reverse
options.rationale: Explains a yield change by a rate argument, treating pressure as acting on one direction only.

options.text: Higher pressure raises the temperature inside the reactor as well
options.rationale: Brings in heating, which would in fact lower the yield, not raise it.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by saying that the Haber reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium?

options.text: Both reactions have stopped, so nothing changes
options.rationale: Unchanging amounts look exactly like a reaction that has finished.

options.text: The amounts of reactants and products are equal
options.rationale: 'Equilibrium' is read as equal quantities rather than equal rates.

options.text: All of the nitrogen and hydrogen has been used up
options.rationale: Treats equilibrium as the end point of a reaction that goes to completion.

options.text: The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates
options.rationale: At equilibrium in a closed system both reactions continue, but at the same rate, so the amounts stay constant.

mcqs.stem: In the Haber process the ammonia is removed as soon as it liquefies. What effect does this have on the equilibrium?

options.text: It shifts to the left, so less ammonia is made overall
options.rationale: Reads the snapshot - less ammonia present - as the final outcome.

options.text: It stops, because a product has been taken away
options.rationale: Treats equilibrium as a fixed state that breaks when it is disturbed.

options.text: It has no effect, as only rate has been changed
options.rationale: Assigns every change in the plant to rate rather than to position of equilibrium.

options.text: It shifts to the right, so more ammonia is formed
options.rationale: Removing a product means the system responds by producing more of it, so more raw material is converted.

mcqs.stem: Why is a temperature of about 450°C used, rather than a much lower temperature?

options.text: A lower temperature gives a lower yield and also a slower rate
options.rationale: Assumes yield follows rate, so cooling is thought to be bad for both.

options.text: A lower temperature would raise the yield and the rate together
options.rationale: Assumes both graphs move the same way, so no compromise would be needed.

options.text: A lower temperature gives a higher yield, but the rate is too slow
options.rationale: 450°C is a compromise: the yield is sacrificed to obtain ammonia at a commercially useful rate.

options.text: A lower temperature would stop the iron catalyst working at all
options.rationale: Explains the choice by the catalyst rather than by the trade-off it is meant to illustrate.

mcqs.stem: Raising the temperature of the Haber process increases the rate of production. What is the cost of doing this?

options.text: There is no cost, because a higher temperature raises the yield too
options.rationale: Applies the rates rule to equilibrium and concludes that heating has no drawback.

options.text: The equilibrium shifts further towards ammonia, wasting the raw gas
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the shift wrong and then misreads it as a disadvantage.

options.text: The iron catalyst is used up more quickly at high temperatures
options.rationale: Treats the catalyst as a reactant that is consumed faster when heated.

options.text: A smaller percentage of the nitrogen and hydrogen becomes ammonia
options.rationale: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating moves the equilibrium back towards the reactants.

mcqs.stem: Why is a pressure of about 200 atmospheres used rather than a far higher pressure?

options.text: Very high pressures would lower the yield of the ammonia
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the pressure effect on equilibrium the wrong way round.

options.text: Very high pressures need costly equipment and are less safe
options.rationale: The chemistry favours higher pressure, but stronger vessels and larger compressors cost more than the extra ammonia is worth.

options.text: Very high pressures have no further effect on the yield
options.rationale: Assumes pressure acts only on rate, so raising it further would be pointless.

options.text: Very high pressures would slow the reaction down too much
options.rationale: Reasons that squashed particles move less freely, so the reaction must slow.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the raw materials and energy used in the Haber process is correct?

options.text: Nitrogen comes from the air, but hydrogen and energy both cost money
options.rationale: Availability and cost differ: air is free, but hydrogen from natural gas and the energy for heating and compressing must be paid for.

options.text: Both raw materials are free, so the only cost is the equipment
options.rationale: 'Nitrogen comes from the air' is generalised to both gases.

options.text: The gases are recycled, so no more raw materials are needed at all
options.rationale: Forgets that the nitrogen and hydrogen leaving as ammonia must be replaced.

options.text: Energy is free because the forward reaction gives out heat energy
options.rationale: Assumes an exothermic reaction pays for its own heating and compression.

mcqs.stem: The commercially used conditions for the Haber process are chosen because they

options.text: give the greatest possible yield of ammonia, whatever it may cost
options.rationale: Optimises one variable and ignores rate, safety and cost.

options.text: give the fastest rate possible, because the yield does not matter
options.rationale: Assumes recycling makes yield irrelevant, so only speed is worth optimising.

options.text: give an acceptable yield, at an acceptable rate, for an acceptable cost
options.rationale: The conditions balance position of equilibrium, rate, and the cost of raw materials and energy.

options.text: give the lowest possible energy bill, whatever the rate may be
options.rationale: Optimises cost alone, which would mean a cold reactor producing almost nothing.

mcqs.stem: What must an NPK fertiliser contain?

options.text: The elements nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
options.rationale: Reads the letters NPK as the elements themselves rather than their compounds.

options.text: Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
options.rationale: NPK fertilisers contain compounds of all three elements.

options.text: A single compound containing all three elements
options.rationale: Treats the fertiliser as one substance rather than a formulation of several salts.

options.text: Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and calcium
options.rationale: Calcium appears throughout this topic in calcium nitrate and calcium phosphate, so it displaces potassium.

mcqs.stem: A crop is short of potassium. Which substance would supply it?

options.text: Potassium metal, which is spread onto the soil as it is
options.rationale: Reads 'potassium' on the label as the element rather than as a compound of it.

options.text: Phosphate rock, which is mined and used without treatment
options.rationale: Picks a mined material, missing both that it is insoluble and that it supplies phosphorus.

options.text: Potassium sulfate, a soluble salt obtained by mining
options.rationale: Potassium sulfate is mined and is soluble, so it can be used as a fertiliser directly.

options.text: Ammonium nitrate, a soluble salt made from ammonia
options.rationale: A genuine fertiliser and a soluble salt, but it supplies nitrogen, not potassium.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that an NPK fertiliser is a formulation?

options.text: It is a single compound made in one reaction vessel
options.rationale: Treats the bag of fertiliser as one substance with one formula.

options.text: It is a solution of the three elements dissolved in water
options.rationale: Combines the element misconception with an assumption that fertiliser must be liquid.

options.text: It is a pure salt that has been ground down to a powder
options.rationale: Recognises it as a salt but not that several different salts are blended.

options.text: It is a mixture of salts, blended in measured quantities
options.rationale: NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.

mcqs.stem: Why is the industrial production of NPK fertilisers described as several integrated processes?

options.text: One continuous reaction turns the raw materials into fertiliser
options.rationale: Expects a single industrial process to be represented by a single reaction.

options.text: Different salts are made in linked stages on the same site
options.rationale: A variety of raw materials are used in several processes that feed into one another, and the salts are then blended.

options.text: Every salt in the fertiliser is made in a separate factory
options.rationale: Recognises that several salts are needed but misses that the processes are linked on one site.

options.text: The fertiliser is one compound made in one step from rock
options.rationale: Combines the single-compound idea with a single-step process.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about making ammonium nitrate from ammonia is correct?

options.text: Ammonium nitrate forms when ammonia reacts with nitrogen gas
options.rationale: The name 'nitrate' is matched to nitrogen gas rather than to the acid that supplies it.

options.text: Ammonium nitrate forms when ammonium reacts with nitric acid
options.rationale: Swaps the neutral molecule ammonia for the ammonium ion found in the product.

options.text: Ammonium nitrate forms when ammonia reacts with nitric acid
options.rationale: Ammonia is a base neutralised by nitric acid: NH3 + HNO3 → NH4NO3.

options.text: Ammonium nitrate and water form from ammonia and nitric acid
options.rationale: Applies 'acid + base → salt + water' to ammonia, which contains no oxygen to form water.

mcqs.stem: Which salt is formed when ammonia is neutralised by sulfuric acid?

options.text: Ammonium sulfide
options.rationale: The salt is named by ear from 'sulfuric' rather than from the sulfate ion.

options.text: Ammonium sulfite
options.rationale: Sulfite belongs to sulfurous acid, not sulfuric acid.

options.text: Ammonia sulfate
options.rationale: Uses the name of the neutral molecule where the name of the ion is needed.

options.text: Ammonium sulfate
options.rationale: Sulfuric acid contains the sulfate ion, so its ammonium salt is ammonium sulfate.

mcqs.stem: Phosphate rock is mined. Why can it not be spread onto fields as a fertiliser?

options.text: It contains no phosphorus until an acid has been added to it
options.rationale: Credits the acid with supplying the phosphorus instead of releasing it.

options.text: It is insoluble, so plants cannot take it in through their roots
options.rationale: Phosphate rock cannot be used directly; it must be converted into soluble salts first.

options.text: It can be spread straight onto fields once it is ground down
options.rationale: Treats phosphate rock like the mined potassium salts, which can be used directly.

options.text: It is too acidic for crops until it has been neutralised first
options.rationale: Reverses the chemistry: acid is added to the rock, not removed from it.

mcqs.stem: Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are obtained by mining. How are they used in NPK fertilisers?

options.text: They are treated with nitric acid in order to make them soluble
options.rationale: Generalises the acid treatment of phosphate rock to every mined material.

options.text: They are heated with phosphate rock to make one compound
options.rationale: Assumes a single reaction combines the raw materials into the finished product.

options.text: They are used directly, because they are soluble salts
options.rationale: Unlike phosphate rock, these mined salts dissolve in water, so no further treatment is needed.

options.text: They are treated with ammonia to add nitrogen to them first
options.rationale: Assumes every raw material must be reacted with something before it is useful.

mcqs.stem: Why is phosphate rock treated with nitric acid or sulfuric acid?

options.text: To add extra phosphorus into the fertiliser
options.rationale: Assumes the acid is the source of the phosphorus.

options.text: To turn it into salts that dissolve in water
options.rationale: The acids produce soluble salts that can be used as fertilisers.

options.text: To break it down into its separate elements
options.rationale: Assumes plants need the elements themselves rather than soluble compounds.

options.text: To make the fertiliser acidic so it kills weeds
options.rationale: Confuses a fertiliser with a herbicide, prompted by the word 'acid'.

mcqs.stem: Which products are formed when phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid?

options.text: Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
options.rationale: Nitric acid gives phosphoric acid together with the soluble salt calcium nitrate.

options.text: Phosphoric acid and solid calcium sulfate
options.rationale: Keeps the memorable product, phosphoric acid, but attaches the sulfuric acid by-product to it.

options.text: Calcium phosphate and calcium nitrate
options.rationale: Borrows the superphosphate answer and applies it to the wrong acid.

options.text: Ammonium nitrate and calcium phosphate
options.rationale: Brings in the ammonium salt from elsewhere in the fertiliser topic.

mcqs.stem: Treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid produces single superphosphate. What is single superphosphate?

options.text: A mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium nitrate
options.rationale: Swaps in the by-product that belongs to the nitric acid route.

options.text: A mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
options.rationale: Sulfuric acid leaves calcium sulfate alongside the calcium phosphate, so the product is a mixture.

options.text: Phosphoric acid mixed with solid calcium sulfate
options.rationale: Assumes any acid on phosphate rock produces phosphoric acid.

options.text: A single compound, calcium sulfate, on its own
options.rationale: Expects one product rather than a mixture, and drops the phosphorus altogether.

mcqs.stem: Which acid is used to treat phosphate rock to make triple superphosphate, and what is triple superphosphate?

options.text: Sulfuric acid, giving solid calcium phosphate
options.rationale: Matches 'triple' with the acid that sounds strongest.

options.text: Nitric acid, giving calcium phosphate
options.rationale: Chooses the acid whose route actually produces phosphoric acid, reversing the two.

options.text: Phosphoric acid, giving calcium phosphate
options.rationale: Phosphoric acid produces triple superphosphate, which is calcium phosphate.

options.text: Sulfuric acid, giving calcium sulfate
options.rationale: Names the by-product of the sulfuric acid route as the fertiliser itself.

mcqs.stem: A student prepares ammonium sulfate in the laboratory. How does this differ from industrial production of the same salt?

options.text: The laboratory uses dilute solutions in a small batch process
options.rationale: The laboratory route titrates dilute ammonia against dilute acid and crystallises a pure salt, one batch at a time.

options.text: The laboratory runs one continuous process from raw materials
options.rationale: Describes the industrial arrangement and attaches it to the laboratory.

options.text: The laboratory uses the same method, just on a smaller scale
options.rationale: Assumes the industrial process is the laboratory method scaled up.

options.text: The laboratory needs no titration, as purity does not matter
options.rationale: Reverses the requirement: it is industry that does not need a pure crystalline salt.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the industrial manufacture of ammonium nitrate is correct?

options.text: Hot concentrated solutions of ammonia and nitric acid are reacted
options.rationale: Industry runs the neutralisation continuously with concentrated solutions, on a very large scale.

options.text: Dilute solutions are titrated, then the salt is crystallised out
options.rationale: Transfers the laboratory preparation directly to the industrial plant.

options.text: The reaction produces ammonium nitrate and water in equal amounts
options.rationale: Applies 'acid + base → salt + water' to ammonia, which has no oxygen to give.

options.text: The ammonium nitrate is mined and then treated with nitric acid
options.rationale: Assumes fertiliser salts are dug out of the ground, as phosphate rock is.
